html:
The map's label, in 1783 and 1800, for the lands of Dutch-speaking settlers in the interior of the Cape Colony, in what is now South Africa. Most were trekboers: farmers who grazed cattle and sheep across the dry Karoo and kept moving their farms further from Cape Town.

The colony had begun in 1652 as a supply post of the Dutch East India Company. As settlers spread inland they took the grazing land, water and herds of the Khoikhoi and San. Many Khoikhoi died of smallpox or ended up working on settler farms, and San hunters were killed in long frontier fighting.

By the 1770s the frontier had reached the Fish River, where it met the Xhosa, and the first of a century of frontier wars broke out in 1779. Britain took the Cape in 1795, and many of these farmers' grandchildren later left on the Great Trek.
